idiom_name: no runtime reader-writer lock; Readonly<T> access-mode split plus single-owner state (Web Locks 'shared'/'exclusive' across workers)
implementation_notes: TypeScript compiles to the same single-threaded runtime as JavaScript, so there is nothing to synchronise inside a realm and no blocking primitive to build a reader-writer lock from; what TypeScript adds is a compile-time access-mode split - readers receive Readonly<T> views, writers keep the mutable type, and the boundary between them is a module or worker that owns the state. Cross-realm coordination is asynchronous: Web Locks with mode: 'shared' for readers and 'exclusive' for the writer, or an Atomics gate inside workers, where Atomics.wait is legal. The classic lock is justified only for a worker that must block on a SharedArrayBuffer; the typed single-owner design replaces it everywhere else.
pitfalls: Readonly<T> is erased at runtime: a cast (as any) or an untyped boundary can mutate the 'read-only' view; Object.freeze only helps where the value is created.
Object.freeze is shallow - nested objects stay mutable unless every level is frozen, so DeepReadonly<T> types and runtime freezing must agree.
A promise-chain or Web Locks mutex does not protect synchronous interleaving between awaits; state changed in one tick is visible to readers in the next.
SharedArrayBuffer needs cross-origin isolation headers in browsers, so code that 'just works' in Node fails in the browser.
alternative: Keep the mutable state inside one owner (the event loop, a module singleton, or a single worker) and hand readers a Readonly<T> view or an immutable snapshot; serialise writers asynchronously with a promise-chain mutex or the Web Locks API (mode 'shared' for readers, 'exclusive' for the writer); use SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics only inside workers when memory really must be shared.
